title: vpc-firewall-policies-and-dns-tf-modules-draft
content:
Context:

This is a working draft for network-specific playbooks and Terraform module notes focused on on-prem / VPC private deployments. The goals are: ensure predictable private DNS behavior (split-horizon / conditional forwarders), define safe ingress/egress patterns (including NAT strategies for egress allowlisting), and formalize firewall and k8s network policy defaults. Also includes a migration/upgrade plan for Terraform modules and state changes that touch network resources.

Assumptions and scope:
- Customers may run Redwood Private in a VPC (cloud) or in on-prem racks behind customer firewalls and load balancers.
- We do not assume customer-managed DNS is always reachable from pods; we must support two common patterns: 1) Forwarding to customer resolvers via peering/VPN, 2) Hosting a local resolver (CoreDNS) that forwards out.
- We must support egress NAT patterns required by customers that maintain external allowlists (fixed egress IPs).
- This doc does not replace vendor-specific firewall guides (Palo Alto / Fortinet / Cisco).

Design goals (networking):
- Predictable DNS resolution for service discovery and private hosted zones.
- Minimal wide-open egress; default-deny with a small allowlist for necessary services.
- Clear migration path for TF module upgrades and resource renames without dropping traffic.

High-level recommendations (short):
- Use split-horizon private zones for internal domains (redwood.internal or customer-specific), and conditional forwarders to customer DNS servers for customer-owned zones.
- Run a small HA CoreDNS pair on the private control plane (or forward to customer resolvers via VPN).
- Provide two egress models: NAT gateway (single egress IP) and SNAT on-prem appliance (for customers that need fixed IPs). Support both with TF flags.
- Default firewall posture: deny all ingress, allow only: 443 (app LB from customer), 9000-9100 (internal control plane), 53 TCP/UDP only between resolver endpoints, and management ports (SSH) limited by source lists.

Terraform module notes (summary):
- Modules to touch: modules/network/vpc, modules/network/dns, modules/network/firewall, modules/network/egress-nat.
- Current state: many customers use older tf modules (v0.1.x) referenced via tag in git. We are preparing v0.3.0 with breaking rename of resource names for firewall policies to align with new schema.

Module design patterns and HCL snippets (for engineers):
- Example module invocation (preferred pattern):

module "private_dns" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com:redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//modules/network/dns?ref=v0.3.0"
  cluster_id = var.cluster_id
  dns_domain = var.private_domain # e.g., "redwood.internal"
  forwarders = var.customer_dns_ips # list of IPs for conditional forwarders
  ha_count = 2
}

module "egress_nat" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com:redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//modules/network/egress-nat?ref=v0.3.0"
  mode = var.egress_mode # "nat-gateway" | "customer-appliance"
  allowed_destinations = var.egress_allowlist
  public_ip = var.allocated_public_ip # optional, used for static egress IPs
}

Notes about stateful renames: when renaming resources in v0.3.0 we will ship a migration script in the repo root called tf-state-migration.sh that runs the required terraform state mv commands. Example commands that will be in the migration script:

# run in module dir after bumping module ref and terraform init -upgrade
terraform state mv module.old_firewall.aws_security_group.old_name module.new_firewall.aws_security_group.new_name
terraform state mv module.old_dns.aws_route53_record.old module.new_dns.aws_route53_record.new

If resources cannot be renamed, the script will attempt an import with terraform import. All migration steps are gated behind a dry-run flag and must be executed during a planned maintenance window.

Private DNS specifics:
- Pattern A (Forwarding): Deploy CoreDNS as a pair within the control plane. CoreDNS config has conditional forwarders for: customer domains (e.g., corp.example.com) -> customer resolver IPs over VPN/peering. Upstream fallback to provider resolvers (when allowed).
- Pattern B (Peered Resolver): Point cluster resolv.conf to customer VPC resolver IPs (e.g., 169.254.169.253 style resolvers) via DHCP or kubelet config. Use this only when peering and routing are stable.

CoreDNS example config (conceptual):

# Corefile snippet
redwood.internal:53 {
    file /etc/coredns/redwood.internal.db
    log
}

corp.example.com:53 {
    forward . 10.1.2.3 10.1.2.4
    policy sequential
}

. {
    forward . 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4
    cache 30
}

Operational notes for DNS:
- Healthcheck endpoints for CoreDNS must be enabled and probed by the control plane health monitor; if both CoreDNS pods fail, fall back to node-level resolvers before failing requests.
- TTLs: keep internal zone TTLs low (30–300s) for fast updates during failover.
- DNS logging: turn on query logging in debug for troubleshooting but keep it off by default in production.

Ingress/Egress patterns and firewall defaults:
- Ingress: Customers will control external ingress to app load balancers. We only document internal control-plane ingress rules:
  - Allow from customer load balancer IP ranges to app ports 443/80 (TLS termination location varies).
  - Allow kubelet health and control plane traffic across expected ports (6443, 10250, 2379-2380 for etcd if exposed).
- Egress: Default deny egress from workloads. Egress should be implemented via a shared egress service or NAT gateway. Two supported approaches:
  1) Central NAT gateway: All egress SNATed to one (or small pool) of public IPs managed by Redwood. Good for customers needing simple allowlist maintenance.
  2) Customer appliance: Route egress to a customer-managed NAT/firewall appliance (preferred for high-security customers).

Firewall rule examples (policy-first):
- Minimal required rules (control plane):
  - Allow: control-plane-management-subnet -> control-plane-3.0.0.0/24 : TCP 22 (SSH) [admin only]
  - Allow: LB -> app-subnet : TCP 443
  - Allow: pods -> dns-resolver-subnet : UDP/TCP 53
  - Deny: app-subnet -> 0.0.0.0/0 : ALL (default deny)

Kubernetes network policy examples (YAML snippets as text):

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress","Egress"]

# allow dns to kube-system dns pods
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-to-kube-dns
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53

Operational playbook for upgrades (Terraform modules):
1) Preparation (2+ days before maintenance):
   - Announce maintenance window to customer and SRE.
   - Run terraform plan with module ref bumped locally and capture diff.
   - Run the provided tf-state-migration.sh in dry-run mode, validate state mv commands.
   - Create rollback PR which pins old module ref and contains state mv reversal steps.

2) Maintenance window steps:
   - Lock state (remote state locking service, e.g., DynamoDB) and take a backup of tfstate snapshot.
   - terraform init -upgrade in a separate workspace for the customer.
   - Apply DNS module first (HA CoreDNS changes). Confirm CoreDNS pods healthy and serving internal zones.
   - Apply firewall/egress changes next but in canary: apply to a staging/non-critical cluster or small subset of subnets.
   - Monitor logs, DNS metrics, and egress flow (tcpdump/flow logs) for 30 minutes after each step.

3) Rollout and verification:
   - After canary success, rollout across remaining clusters/subnets in batched windows.
   - Re-run tf-state-migration script if any manual state moves are required during the rollout.

Rollback plan (if DNS or egress breaks):
- Immediate: revert firewall/egress TF apply by applying the pinned rollback workspace.
- If DNS breaks and cannot be quickly fixed: reconfigure kubelets/nodes to point to node-local resolvers or customer resolver IPs (temporary fix) and revert TF changes.
- Postmortem required within 48 hours.

Testing checklist prior to upgrades (pre-flight):
- Plan: terraform plan shows only expected changes; no destructive deletes unless explicitly noted.
- DNS: validate zone files and forwarders in staging; check NXDOMAIN behavior and split-horizon resolution.
- Egress: validate that services that require fixed egress IPs still see the old IP (use curl iflist.akamai.com or similar).
- Firewall: run rule simulator (vendor) if available; otherwise, maintain a short maintenance window to revert.

Monitoring and observability we must have enabled for upgrades:
- DNS query logs and resolver health metrics (CoreDNS Prometheus).
- VPC flow logs / firewall logs aggregated into ELK.
- K8s network policy deny hits (Cilium/Calico counters) and pod-level egress errors.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Should we make the CoreDNS deployment optional by default, or enable it for all Private installs? (ops preference: enable by default, allow opt-out in var).
- How to surface per-customer egress IP allocations in the Console? (need product + UI input).
- Can we create an automated TF test harness to run terraform apply/plan against a lightweight emulator for common vendor firewalls?

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Finalize v0.3.0 module schema and add migration script to repo.
- [ ] Add automated CI plan that runs terraform plan with the new ref for each customer workspace and flags unexpected diffs. (Owner: Ravi)
- [ ] Draft customer communication template for maintenance windows touching network resources. (Owner: Leah)
- [ ] Add example network policy library to modules repo for common app patterns. (Owner: Jonas)

Appendix: quick commands (ops cheatsheet)
- Bump module ref locally and test plan:
  git checkout -b tf-bump-dns-v0.3.0
  sed -i 's/ref=v0.2.1/ref=v0.3.0/g' modules/*.tf
  terraform init -upgrade
  terraform plan -var-file=customer.tfvars

- Running a state move (example):
  terraform state mv module.old_dns.aws_route53_record.old_name module.new_dns.aws_route53_record.new_name

- Emergency revert (apply pinned rollback workspace):
  terraform workspace select customer-rollback
  terraform apply -var-file=rollback.tfvars -auto-approve

Notes for SRE handoff:
- Document the exact maintenance steps and the list of affected customers upfront.
- Ensure TF state snapshot is uploaded to secure S3 with versioned key before starting.

If you have customer-specific constraints (e.g., forbid any outbound to public resolvers), call that out in the customer.tfvars and the module will switch to "peered-resolver" mode.

End of draft.

Feedback welcome — leave inline comments or push updates to the PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules/pull/58
